"'''You're Makin' Me High'''" is a song by American singer [[Toni Braxton]], released in May 1996, by [[LaFace Records|LaFace]] and [[Arista Records]], as the [[lead single]] from her second [[studio album]], ''[[Secrets (Toni Braxton album)|Secrets]]'' (1996). The mid-tempo song represents a joint collaboration between the [[Grammy Award]]-winning producer [[Babyface (musician)|Babyface]] and [[Bryce Wilson]]. The beat of the song was originally for singer-songwriter [[Brandy (singer)|Brandy]], with Dallas Austin pegged to write a lyric to override; however, Braxton had Babyface write lyrics for the song. It was ultimately issued in the United States as a [[A-side and B-side#Double A-side|double A-side]] with "[[Let It Flow (song)|Let It Flow]]", the [[Airplay (radio)|airplay]] hit from the 1995 film ''[[Waiting to Exhale]]''. 

"You're Makin' Me High" became Braxton's first number-one single on both the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and [[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs|Hot R&B Singles]] charts; it remained on top for one week on the former and for two weeks on the latter, eventually reaching [[RIAA certification|platinum]] status. The accompanying music video was directed by [[Bille Woodruff]]. A [[remix]] of the song by [[David Morales]] with re-recorded vocals allowed the single to also top the [[Dance Club Songs|Dance Club Play]] chart for two weeks in August 1996. Another remix for urban markets was created featuring rapper [[Foxy Brown (rapper)|Foxy Brown]], called the "Groove Mix". A [[dancehall]] mix was also recorded featuring Jamaican dancehall DJ [[Mad Cobra]].

The song earned Braxton her third [[Grammy Award for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance]] in [[Grammy Awards of 1997|1997]]. The success of "You're Makin' Me High" would later be continued with the release of "[[Un-Break My Heart]]". "You're Makin' Me High" was [[Sampling (music)|sampled]] for [[Method Man & Redman]]'s 2001 song "Part II", from the ''[[How High]]'' soundtrack. In 2014, Anglo-American producer/DJ [[Secondcity]] sampled a part of the song's bridge for the main hook of his UK number-one single "[[I Wanna Feel]]".

"You're Makin' Me High" is a song by American singer Toni Braxton, released in May 1996, by LaFace and Arista Records, as the lead single from her second studio album, Secrets (1996). The mid-tempo song represents a joint collaboration between the Grammy Award-winning producer Babyface and Bryce Wilson. The beat of the song was originally for singer-songwriter Brandy, with Dallas Austin pegged to write a lyric to override; however, Braxton had Babyface write lyrics for the song. It was ultimately issued in the United States as a double A-side with "Let It Flow", the airplay hit from the 1995 film Waiting to Exhale. 

"You're Makin' Me High" became Braxton's first number-one single on both the US Billboard Hot 100 and Hot R&B Singles charts; it remained on top for one week on the former and for two weeks on the latter, eventually reaching platinum status. The accompanying music video was directed by Bille Woodruff. A remix of the song by David Morales with re-recorded vocals allowed the single to also top the Dance Club Play chart for two weeks in August 1996. Another remix for urban markets was created featuring rapper Foxy Brown, called the "Groove Mix". A dancehall mix was also recorded featuring Jamaican dancehall DJ Mad Cobra.

The song earned Braxton her third Grammy Award for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance in 1997. The success of "You're Makin' Me High" would later be continued with the release of "Un-Break My Heart". "You're Makin' Me High" was sampled for Method Man & Redman's 2001 song "Part II", from the How High soundtrack. In 2014, Anglo-American producer/DJ Secondcity sampled a part of the song's bridge for the main hook of his UK number-one single "I Wanna Feel".

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
[[Larry Flick]] from ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine described the song a "sleek'n'sexy slice o' [[Funk|jeep funk]]" with a "sophisticated toned and rich production", as well as praising the song's chorus.<ref name="Pop">{{Cite magazine |last=Flick |first=Larry |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uA0EAAAAMBAJ |title=Reviews & Previews: Singles - Pop |date=May 18, 1996 |magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |pages=70 |author-link=Larry Flick}}</ref> Peter Miro from ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' remarked that Braxton "oozes sensuality with her phrasing on 'You're Makin' Me High', mated to tight, cascading backup harmonies, and a crossover-capable bass line. She projects allure sufficient enough to perpetuate her sultry, waif-like mystique."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Peter|last=Miro|title=Urban: Urban Singles Reviews|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/90s/1996/CB-1996-06-29.pdf|magazine=[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]|date=June 29, 1996|page=13|accessdate=November 12, 2022}}</ref> Alan Jones from ''[[Music Week]]'' declared it as "a nagging and surprisingly sprightly [[Contemporary R&B|R&B]] workout", with the singer's "exceptional" vocals and deemed it "an obvious hit".<ref name="R&B">{{cite magazine|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1996/Music-Week-1996-07-06.pdf|first=Alan|last=Jones|title=Talking Music|magazine=[[Music Week]]|date=July 6, 1996|page=10|accessdate=September 1, 2021}}</ref> 

Damien Mendis from the ''RM'' Dance Update gave the song a full score of five out of five, writing, "Oh my gosh! The ever-reliable [[Babyface (musician)|Babyface]] hooks up with [[Bryce Wilson]] of [[Groove Theory]] to create a definitive true R&B flave that'll leave you begging for more. Check the recipe: phat '[[Tell Me (Groove Theory song)|Tell Me]]'-style beats, Intro/[[Edie Brickell]]-ish guitar licks entwined with subtle bass and a floating eastern-sounding moog hook. Toni's effortlessly smooth vocal is textured beautifully with lushly layered backing harmonies. Delicious!"<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1996/Music-Week-1996-06-29.pdf|first=Damien|last=Mendis|title=Hot Vinyl|magazine=[[Music Week]], in [[Record Mirror]] (Dance Update Supplemental Insert)|date=June 29, 1996|page=6|accessdate=August 22, 2021}}</ref> In a retrospective review, Pop Rescue complimented it as a "wonderful mid-tempo song, making the most of the sultry vocals, slinky bass and beats." The reviewer also added that the backing vocals "sound great – adding an extra layer of warmth."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://poprescue.com/2015/11/27/pop-rescue-secrets-by-toni-braxton-cd-1997/|title=Review: "Secrets" by Toni Braxton (CD, 1997)|publisher=Pop Rescue|date=November 27, 2015|access-date=April 14, 2020}}</ref> Richard Harrington from ''[[The Washington Post]]'' stated that Braxton "can handle airy, upbeat material", like "You're Makin' Me High". He explained, "With its sinewy synth-line, it has more of a [[West Coast hip hop|West Coast]] sound than most [[LaFace Records|LaFace]] productions, but the impression is more joyful than ominous. A celebration of sexual desire, it also includes a bit of erotic breathing and a coy [[masturbation]] reference".<ref name="harrington"/>
sections.text:
Larry Flick from Billboard magazine described the song a "sleek'n'sexy slice o' jeep funk" with a "sophisticated toned and rich production", as well as praising the song's chorus. Peter Miro from Cash Box remarked that Braxton "oozes sensuality with her phrasing on 'You're Makin' Me High', mated to tight, cascading backup harmonies, and a crossover-capable bass line. She projects allure sufficient enough to perpetuate her sultry, waif-like mystique." Alan Jones from Music Week declared it as "a nagging and surprisingly sprightly R&B workout", with the singer's "exceptional" vocals and deemed it "an obvious hit". 

Damien Mendis from the RM Dance Update gave the song a full score of five out of five, writing, "Oh my gosh! The ever-reliable Babyface hooks up with Bryce Wilson of Groove Theory to create a definitive true R&B flave that'll leave you begging for more. Check the recipe: phat 'Tell Me'-style beats, Intro/Edie Brickell-ish guitar licks entwined with subtle bass and a floating eastern-sounding moog hook. Toni's effortlessly smooth vocal is textured beautifully with lushly layered backing harmonies. Delicious!" In a retrospective review, Pop Rescue complimented it as a "wonderful mid-tempo song, making the most of the sultry vocals, slinky bass and beats." The reviewer also added that the backing vocals "sound great – adding an extra layer of warmth." Richard Harrington from The Washington Post stated that Braxton "can handle airy, upbeat material", like "You're Makin' Me High". He explained, "With its sinewy synth-line, it has more of a West Coast sound than most LaFace productions, but the impression is more joyful than ominous. A celebration of sexual desire, it also includes a bit of erotic breathing and a coy masturbation reference".

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext:
{{Unreferenced section|date=May 2014}}
The music video for "You're Makin' Me High", directed by American director [[Bille Woodruff]], features Braxton and a group of friends (consisting of actresses [[Erika Alexander]], [[Vivica A. Fox]], and [[Tisha Campbell]]) enjoying themselves in luxurious surroundings. An elevator brings up a series of men. Braxton and her friends "judge" the men using oversized playing cards as score cards. Periodically, one of the women chooses a man to leave with. Braxton chooses [[Bryce Wilson]], whom she dated at the time, and they are shown together in a bathtub of [[cotton candy]] and on a dance floor, with Braxton also shown wearing a white bodysuit.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-20 |title=The Number Ones: Toni Braxton's "You're Makin' Me High" |url=https://stereogum.com/2183763/the-number-ones-toni-braxtons-youre-makin-me-high/columns/the-number-ones/ |access-date=2026-07-28 |website=stereogum.com |language=en}}</ref> The music video premiered on [[MTV]], [[BET]], and [[VH1]] on the week ending May 5, 1996.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uA0EAAAAMBAJ |title=Video Monitor |date=May 18, 1996 |publisher=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |pages=81}}</ref>

Periodically, one of the women chooses a man to leave with. Braxton chooses Bryce Wilson, whom she dated at the time, and they are shown together in a bathtub of cotton candy and on a dance floor, with Braxton also shown wearing a white bodysuit. The music video premiered on MTV, BET, and VH1 on the week ending May 5, 1996.
